newsitem.title: USA: Looted Dutch gold in Swiss commercial banks - papers.
newsitem.headline: Looted Dutch gold in Swiss commercial banks - papers.

text.p: Swiss commercial banks received deposits of gold looted by Nazis during the Second World War contrary to claims that only the central bank dealt with the German Reichsbank on gold, according to classified U.S. Treasury Department documents released on Monday.
The documents show that the Basler Handelsbank and the Swiss Bank Corp., both of Zurich, received gold bars worth $2 million during the war, about $20 million by 1996 prices.

The documents, released by the World Jewish Congress (WJC), which is spearheading a search of U.S. National Archives, state that the gold in the two banks was looted by the Germans from the Netherlands.

Private Swiss banks have strongly insisted that commercial banks in Switzerland did not receive looted gold from the Nazis. They said that the Swiss Central Bank did, however, as payments for goods and services. They also received gold as payment for purchases made by the Allies.

"These documents show that there was no Berlin Wall separating transactions made by the Swiss Central Bank and the private banks as Swiss bankers have claimed," WJC Vice President Kalman Sultanik said.
Sultanik also renewed his charges that the Swiss Ombudsman who has been handling claims made by Holocaust survivors or their relatives was engaging in a cruel hoax.
The Ombudsman has scheduled a news conference for Tuesday on whether the Swiss had located any dormant accounts that might have been held by Holocaust victims.

The WJC said its researchers had found documents in Hungarian diplomatic archives that show that in 1974, Switzerland transferred 400,000 Swiss francs to Budapest to settle claims on heirless assets that Hungarian citizens had deposited in Swiss Banks, while at the same time receiving 500,000 francs from the Hungarians to pay for property nationalised by Budapest that belonged to Swiss citizens.

A similiar deal with Poland revealed this year led to much criticism of the Swiss government from Jewish groups who claimed the Swiss were indirectly compensating their citizens with assets of Holocaust victims.
